title: How Thawte Turned From Web Consulting to Certificates in a Garage
dek: In 1995 a Cape Town student started an internet consultancy in his parents' garage, followed a gap left by US export rules, and ended up vouching for websites.

story.event: Turning a student internet consultancy into a secure-server maker and then a certificate authority
story.summary: In 1995, his final year at the University of Cape Town, Mark Shuttleworth started Thawte in his parents' garage as an internet consulting business. Its focus shifted to security for electronic commerce: he built Sioux, an Apache-based secure web server sold outside the United States, and the work drew Thawte into issuing digital certificates, where it became one of the first issuers recognised by Netscape and Microsoft. VeriSign announced its acquisition of Thawte on 20 December 1999 for stock with an aggregate market value of $575 million.
paragraphs: In 1995, his final year studying business science at the University of Cape Town, Mark Shuttleworth started a small company in his parents' garage. He had met the internet at university and, by his own account, was intrigued by what it would change in business and society. He called the company Thawte and began it as an internet consulting business. A later profile says he first meant to design websites, until an interest in internet security drew him into an online discussion group about code and digital certificates.

The focus soon shifted to security for online trade. The United States restricted the export of strong encryption, and Shuttleworth set out to build a secure web server free of those limits. His server, Sioux, was a version of the open-source Apache server, which he extended with a built-in Python interpreter. His biography says Thawte became the first company to sell a full-security encrypted e-commerce server commercially outside the United States. The open-source world, he said later, "played such a critical role in helping me build Thawte."

The server work pulled the company in a second direction, into the certificates that let a browser check who runs a website. Asked years later for his most exciting moment, he chose a night at 2am when his own Python implementation of RSA produced a digital signature that SSLeay, as OpenSSL was then known, would verify. Thawte became one of the first companies that Netscape and Microsoft recognised as a trusted issuer of website certificates, and the Sioux server was later folded into another product as certification became the business.

It stayed small and informal for years. Morgan Collett, who joined in about 1998 as its second software developer after Shuttleworth himself, said the dozen staff then worked out of a house and several flats in Cape Town. On 20 December 1999, VeriSign announced it had acquired Thawte, which it called the world's second-largest provider of website certificates, in exchange for stock with an aggregate market value of $575 million, about R3.5 billion. Shuttleworth stepped down as chief executive after the sale.

quote.text: If there is compulsion on one side, on the other there is pleasure; on the one hand action is spurred on by want, on the other it hies to its natural fulfilment.
quote.source_title: Sadhana: The Realisation of Life, Project Gutenberg eBook #6842
quote.connection: Tagore says work is pushed by want and drawn by pleasure. Thawte had both: a gap that American export rules left open for anyone outside the country, and a student's rush at 2am when code he had written produced a signature that someone else's software accepted.

reflection: Notice where Thawte's direction came from. Shuttleworth did not set out to run a certificate authority. He kept following a gap that showed up in his own work until the side task became the business, and the want behind it was plain: American export rules had left a gap that could be filled from Cape Town.

You may find the same pattern in an ordinary week: the problem you keep returning to because something is missing, and the small moment when a thing you made finally works. Both are worth noticing, and neither has to be dramatic to count.
invitation: Write down the last time something you made worked for the first time, however small, and what gap it filled. Leave the note where you will see it tomorrow morning.

cross_checks.claim: Shuttleworth started Thawte in 1995, his final year at UCT, in his parents' garage
The business shifted from consulting to security, building Sioux, an Apache-based secure server, for sale outside the US
Thawte was one of the first companies recognised by Netscape and Microsoft as a trusted certificate issuer
VeriSign announced on 20 December 1999 that it had acquired Thawte for stock worth $575 million

research_notes: Sale price, checked as asked: VeriSign's own press release of 20 December 1999 says the stock it would issue 'will have an aggregate market value of $575 million', with the exact number of shares set by VeriSign's trading price before closing and the deal subject to South African regulatory approval. The Register (2024) and Wikipedia say VeriSign paid $575 million; the Cape Argus (2011) gives R3.5 billion. These agree; the story uses the press release's wording and the Cape Argus's rand figure. Because the price was fixed in dollars of VeriSign stock, the cash value to Shuttleworth would have moved with the share price; the story does not claim what he realised. Dates: Shuttleworth's own biography and the Cape Argus both say 1995, his final year at UCT; the garage comes from the Cape Argus (whose text is reproduced nearly word for word by Grocott's Mail, so Grocott's is not cited as independent) and Wikipedia. The order of the change of direction (consulting, then a secure server, then certificates) follows his biography and Wikipedia; no source dates the Netscape and Microsoft recognition or the 2am signature, so the story gives no dates for them. The export-restriction context rests on Wikipedia and is implied by his biography's claim of the first such server 'commercially available outside the United States'. The 1998 staff picture is Morgan Collett's recollection in ITWeb (2001), dated 'three years ago'. Funding: no source reports any outside investor, VeriSign called Thawte 'privately held', and Wikipedia describes a stock purchase 'from Shuttleworth', so 'bootstrapped' is a reasonable reading rather than a documented statement. Two widely repeated details are not used: a 1999 Business Report article (blocked to the verifier) quoting him on a possible Nasdaq listing, and reports of bonuses to his household staff. Shuttleworth's biography and the VeriSign release are cited from Internet Archive copies over http, because web.archive.org refused https connections during checking.
